I could not look up 1acc in this condition (pretrained knowledge only, no network). I therefore can't confirm its exact SCOP 1.75 and SCOPe domain identifiers, and I won't invent them. The class of change the question describes is well established. In SCOP 1.75, chain A of an entry like this was often assigned as one domain covering the whole chain (a d1acca_ style identifier, with the chain letter and underscore meaning 'whole chain'). Later SCOPe releases (2.0x and after) re-examined such entries. They split the chain into two or more sub-domains with numbered identifiers (d1acca1, d1acca2, ...), each with its own residue ranges. The new domains may fall in different families, superfamilies or folds. Alternatively, the whole-chain assignment may have hidden a boundary between a core domain and a separate segment or insert. Check the current SCOPe entry for 1acc to get the actual ranges and sccs strings (class.fold.superfamily.family) before relying on any specific split.

What this shows: a domain is an evolutionary and structural module that can be gained, lost, inserted or rearranged independently of the rest of the polypeptide. A PDB chain is an experimental or genetic unit, not an evolutionary one. A chain-level or whole-chain label can merge modules with different ancestry. It can also hide that one half has a homology relationship (superfamily or family) that the other half lacks. A split makes the evolutionary statement more precise. Each domain gets its own class/fold/superfamily/family placement, and homology claims (superfamily means probable common ancestry; family means clear sequence or functional relatedness) apply per domain, not per chain. Fold-level similarity alone does not imply homology.

Effect on homology searches: (1) Use the current SCOPe domain boundaries, not the old 1.75 whole-chain ones, when building queries, templates or benchmark sets. (2) Search with each domain separately, or at least interpret hits by domain-level coverage. A hit that covers only one domain supports homology and function transfer only for that domain, not for the whole chain. (3) Do not carry the old 1.75 classification over to the whole protein. Old chain-level labels can cause wrong full-length transfer, redundant or leaking train/test splits, and wrong representative choices (such as ASTRAL representatives picked from different domain definitions). (4) Multidomain proteins can score high in global alignments through one shared module while the others are unrelated, so check per-domain alignment coverage, E-values and the SCOPe release number. (5) Domain-level homology does not guarantee the same function. Check active-site conservation and the evidence for the specific function independently. Always record which SCOPe release the labels came from, because boundaries and assignments change between releases.
